'''Alfred Schild''' (September 7, 1921 – May 24, 1977) was a leading [[Austrian Americans|Austrian-American]] physicist, who contributed to the [[History of general relativity#Golden age|golden age of general relativity]] (1960–1975).

==Biography==
Schild was born in [[Istanbul]] on September 7, 1921. His parents were [[German language|German]]-speaking [[Viennese Jews]],<ref name="google">{{cite book|title=The Perfect Theory: A Century of Geniuses and the Battle over General Relativity|author=Ferreira, Pedro G.|date=2014|publisher=Houghton Mifflin Harcourt|isbn=9780547554907|url=https://archive.org/details/perfecttheorycen0000ferr|url-access=registration|page=[https://archive.org/details/perfecttheorycen0000ferr/page/114 114]|accessdate=27 March 2019}}</ref> but his early education was in [[England]]. Upon the outbreak of [[World War II]] Schild was interned as an enemy alien, but later allowed to travel to [[Canada]]. In 1944 he earned his B.A. at the [[University of Toronto]], and in 1946 completed his doctorate under the direction of [[Leopold Infeld]]. Schild spent the next eleven years at the [[Carnegie Institute of Technology]], where he helped to develop the first [[atomic clock]]s.

As [[tensor]]s are the language of [[general relativity]], Schild wrote ''Tensor Calculus'' with [[John L. Synge]] as a textbook.<ref>{{cite book |author1=Synge, J. L. |author2=Schild, A. |name-list-style=amp | title=Tensor Calculus  |url=https://archive.org/details/in.ernet.dli.2015.74559 | publisher=[[University of Toronto Press]]| year=1949 | oclc= 6007241 | isbn=0-8020-1031-8}}</ref> According to a reviewer, "The ideas and concepts are given very concisely and thus a wide range of subjects is considered."<ref>John DeCicco (1951 ) [https://projecteuclid.org/euclid.bams/1183516310 Review: J. L. Synge & Alfred Schild ''Tensor Calculus''], ''[[Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society]]'' 57(6):500–2 via [[Project Euclid]]</ref>

In 1957 Schild moved to the [[University of Texas at Austin]]. In 1962 he became [[Ashbel Smith#Memorials|Ashbel Smith Professor]] and founded the Center for Relativity at University of Texas, Austin.<ref>Richard A. Matzner & L. C. Shepley (1982) ''Spacetime and Geometry: The Alfred Smith Lectures'', page ix, [[University of Texas Press]]</ref> [[Engelbert Schücking]] described the recruitment of professors for the Center:
:In 1962 Alfred got me an associate professorship in the Austin mathematics department, and in the summer of 1962, while attending [[Andrzej Trautman]]’s Relativity conference in Warsaw, Poland, … we persuaded [[Roger Penrose]], [[Roy Kerr]], [[Ray Sachs]], [[Jürgen Ehlers]], Luis Bel and others to flock to the newly created center of gravity in Austin.<ref>[[Engelbert Schücking]] (August 1989) [http://imhodge.startlogic.com/pdfs/schucking%20article%20-%20physics%20today.pdf The First Texas Symposium on Relativistic Astrophysics], [[Physics Today]] pages 46 to 52</ref>

In 1965, Schild found the [[Kerr–Schild perturbations|Kerr–Schild form]] of the spacetime metric.

A dramatization of the calculation of the [[Kerr metric]] by [[Roy Kerr]] was written in 2009 by [[Fulvio Melia]].<ref name=FM>[[Fulvio Melia]] (2009) ''Cracking the Einstein Code'', [[University of Chicago Press]] {{ISBN|9780226519517}}</ref> Kerr had invited Schild to his office to calculate angular momentum in a solution to [[Einstein's field equations]]. "Alfred was a kind and cheerful man, with a flock of silvery hair."<ref name=FM/>{{rp|74}} The climax of ''Cracking the Einstein Code'' was expressed as follows:
{{blockquote|While Schild waited patiently in the armchair, Kerr began calculating at his desk...Kerr put down his pencil and looked up...Schild jumped out of his chair beaming. He appeared to be far more excited than Kerr himself and clearly knew what this meant.<ref name=FM/>{{rp|75}}}}

In a 1970 seminar at [[Princeton University]], Schild introduced an important mathematical construction now known as [[Schild's ladder|Schild's Ladder]], which is used in [[differential geometry]].

{{blockquote|Schild clarified and enlarged general relativity through his studies of single-particle motion, quantization, special solutions and the conformal structure of space-time. ... His expositions of tensor analysis and relativity are still among the best and clearest treatments of these subjects.<ref>{{cite journal|author=Schucking, E. L.|author-link=Engelbert Schücking|title=Obituary. Alfred E. Schild|journal=Physics Today|volume=31|issue=3|year=1978|pages=79–80|bibcode=1978PhT....31c..79S|doi=10.1063/1.2994979|doi-access=free}}</ref>}}

Schild died on May 24, 1977, in [[Downer's Grove, Illinois]], of a [[myocardial infarction|heart attack]].<ref>[https://web2.ph.utexas.edu/utphysicshistory/AlfredSchild.html Alfred Schild] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210728012434/https://web2.ph.utexas.edu/utphysicshistory/AlfredSchild.html |date=2021-07-28 }} from Department of Physics, University of Texas at Austin</ref>

==Legacy==
Schild's private papers are archived by the University of Texas.

==In popular culture==
The science fiction novel ''[[Schild's Ladder]]'' by  [[Greg Egan]] drew heavily on concepts introduced or refined by Schild.
